---
title: "Notes on Building Things"
description: "Observations on attention, routine, risk, and making."
date: 2020-05-05
---

## Start before certainty

Successful outcomes are easy to explain backward. We see skill and effort because they are visible. Luck disappears into the story.

Starting early does not defeat luck. It buys more attempts. More attempts mean more failures one can survive and more chances to notice what works. Time is not just a resource; it is sample size.

## Intensity is trainable

Absorption is not merely a personality trait. A craft, practiced without interruption, makes sustained attention easier to enter. Repetition builds familiarity with the state itself: how to begin, how to stay, and how to return after distraction.

The useful skill is not permanent intensity. It is the ability to direct intensity when the work requires it.

## Approval is expensive

When work requires approval from everyone around me, quality becomes secondary. The objective quietly changes from making something good to avoiding disagreement.

Disagreement need not be hostile. It means refusing to outsource decisions that determine the shape of my work or life.

## Build a system small enough to repeat

Large goals are global objectives. Days are local updates. A routine connects the two.

If the daily update is too large, an ordinary interruption breaks the system. A smaller commitment produces less progress today but survives more days. Its advantage appears only after accumulation.

Consistency and ambition are not opposites. Ambition chooses the direction. Consistency keeps applying the update.

## Find the constraint

Complex projects do not advance evenly. Usually one unresolved problem blocks the rest. Doing ten available tasks can feel productive while leaving that constraint untouched.

The useful question is not “What can I finish today?” It is “What is preventing the project from moving?” Breaking that problem into a task small enough for one day is often the real work.

## Work close to feedback

A salary is not the problem. Distance from feedback can be. Work becomes dull when action is separated from consequence and nothing accumulates: not skill, ownership, judgment, or leverage.

Startups are not automatically better, nor are large organizations automatically worse. The better questions are: How quickly can I see what my work changed? Am I learning something scarce? Does the value I create compound beyond the hours I spend?

## Choose the environment

Part of luck is exposure. A place changes the people one meets, the problems one sees, and the standards that feel normal.

Discomfort is useful when it reveals a limit. It is not useful merely because it hurts. The right environment makes complacency difficult without making sustained work impossible.

## Treat fear as a noisy signal

Fear is neither a command nor an enemy. It is a noisy risk detector. When it appears, I can ask what failure it predicts, how likely that failure is, and whether the downside can be reduced.

Sometimes the signal identifies a real flaw. Sometimes it protects the familiar. The task is to tell the two apart.

## Ideas need not be original

Two reliable sources of ideas are problems I repeatedly face and solutions that work elsewhere.

The first comes with evidence: I know the problem exists. A useful test is whether I would pay for a solution. The second is a form of pattern matching. A model that works in one industry or country may work under different constraints after adaptation.

Copying the surface is easy. Understanding the mechanism is the creative part.

## Attention reveals the objective

Attention is finite. News, messages, work, and entertainment continually bid for it. The things that repeatedly win become my objective function in practice, regardless of what I claim to value.

When my stated goals and observed attention disagree, my behavior is the more accurate description.
